summary.text: 地 means “earth” or “ground,” and also land or place. Its received analysis combines 土, which contributes an earth-related meaning, with 也 as a sound component.

formation.text: 地 is analyzed as a phonosemantic compound: 土 contributes an earth-related meaning, while 也 supplies a sound cue. This Han-period analysis does not establish how the earliest form was devised.

components.text: 土 is the left component in the received analysis and contributes the earth-related meaning category.

也 is the right component in the received analysis and serves as a phonetic component. In Zhengzhang Old Chinese reconstructions, its reading is approximately related to 地’s, although their modern Mandarin readings differ. This supports a sound role but does not prove the graph’s original design. The original referent of 也 is uncertain, so it is not treated as a picture within 地.

sound_limitation.text: The comparison is reconstructed, not directly recorded, and does not by itself prove the graph’s original design rationale.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Old Chinese, the reconstructions are approximately related; in modern Mandarin, 地 dì and 也 yě differ.

history.text: A cataloged Western Zhou bronze form has a complex right element identified as 它 in one account. The Shuowen seal-script form has 土 on the left and 也 on the right. The proposal that 它 was later regularized as 也 is an interpretation, not a sequence established by the forms alone.

地 is also discussed alongside 墬. One proposal treats 墬 as an earlier graph for the earth sense, but the relationship could instead involve parallel or replaced graph use; its chronology is unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The received 土-plus-也 analysis is explicit, but earlier forms have competing interpretations. The proposed 它-to-也 graphic history and the graph’s earliest design remain uncertain.

senses.text: The earliest inspectable account describes 地 as the heavy, turbid yin counterpart to heaven and as the place where things are arrayed. This attested account does not establish the word’s hypothetical original meaning.
Cited texts show noun uses for ground, cultivated land, territory, place, and region. They do not establish when each sense arose or a complete sequence of change.

senses.gloss: grammatical particle after an adjective, commonly read de
senses.period: Song citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Song text is cited for 地 following an adjective. This attests the use in that textual tradition, but does not show how it arose from the noun or another form.

senses.period: Yuan citation; exact first use unresolved
senses.text: A Yuan text is cited for a postverbal use glossed as ‘stand there/remain’; its precise relation to other uses of 地 is unclear.

developments.text: Earth or ground and land or territory are documented noun uses, but the stages and dates linking them are unresolved.

One proposal derives the manner particle through a path from “an adjective place” to “in an adjective manner.” Other analyses connect it to 的 or to demonstrative or interrogative forms. No single derivation or full sequence is established.

limitations.text: Citations to classical works do not independently date surviving wording. The earliest attestations and semantic links among noun senses remain unresolved.
The particle’s relation to the noun 地, to 的, or to demonstrative or interrogative forms remains disputed; no single historical pathway is established.

overview.text: 地 means earth or ground, and also land or place. In the received analysis, 土 contributes the earth-related meaning and 也 provides a sound cue; their proposed Old Chinese sound relationship is reconstructed.

components.text: 土 contributes the character’s earth-related meaning.
也 is a sound cue: its reconstructed Old Chinese reading is approximately related to 地’s, though their modern Mandarin readings differ. Its original referent is uncertain.

takeaway.text: 地 also follows adjectives as a particle, but how this use relates to the earth-and-ground noun remains disputed.

relationships.text: In the received analysis of 地, 土 contributes the earth-related meaning category.
The received analysis assigns 也 a sound role, and historical reconstructions support an approximate relationship without proving the graph’s original design.
